key_insight: Eliciting agents' self-predicted success probabilities before, during, and after tasks reveals systematic agentic overconfidence: some agents that only succeed 22% of the time predict 77% success. Surprisingly, coarser pre-execution estimates sometimes discriminate success better than detailed post-execution reviews.
problem_solved: Addresses whether AI agents can accurately predict their own task success (agentic uncertainty) and quantifies miscalibration and overconfidence across different interrogation timings and informational conditions.
method: Elicit success probability estimates from agents at three timepoints: pre-execution, during execution, and post-execution.
Compare predicted probabilities to actual outcomes across tasks and agents to measure calibration, discrimination, and systematic biases (e.g., overconfidence).
Analyze the effect of information content and prompting (including adversarial prompts) on estimates to understand when and why agentic uncertainty appears.
impact: Reveals that deployed agents can be highly overconfident, which has implications for reliability, risk assessment, and human–AI decision workflows. Simple changes in when and how we ask agents for confidence can improve predictive usefulness and trust.
visual_elements: Calibration plot: predicted success probability vs. actual success rate highlighting extreme overconfidence (e.g., predicted 77% vs actual 22%).
Timeline diagram: three interrogation points (pre-, mid-, post-execution) showing differences in information availability and resulting estimates.
Bar/box chart: discrimination and calibration metrics side-by-side for pre vs mid vs post estimates to show where prediction quality is best.
Icon/flow graphic: decision pipeline illustrating risks of overconfident agents in downstream tasks (alerts, human override, automated actions).
paper_authors: Jean Kaddour, Srijan Patel, Gbètondji Dovonon, Leo Richter, Pasquale Minervini
